To resound means to ring out loudly and powerfully — and especially to fill an entire space with sound, so the sound seems to vibrate all around you, coming from every direction at once.

Imagine a single bell struck inside a stone cathedral. The tone doesn't just travel and disappear; it spreads through the whole building, bounces off the walls, and seems to come from everywhere. That enveloping, space-filling quality is exactly what "resound" captures.
How the word works — two patterns

Here, a sound rings out powerfully and spreads through a space:

  • "The gunshot resounded through the forest." — It rang out and echoed through the trees with great force.
  • "Her voice resounded across the empty hall." — It rang through the whole hall, filling it.
  • "The explosion resounded for miles." — The sound echoed and could be heard over a wide area.
2. A place resounds with a sound

This is the most common pattern. The focus is on the space being completely filled by the sound:

  • "The stadium resounded with cheers." — The entire stadium was filled and vibrating with the sound of cheering.
  • "The cave resounded with dripping water." — Every corner of the cave was filled with that sound.
  • "The room resounded with laughter." — Laughter bounced off every wall, filling the space completely.

The preposition "with" tells you what kind of sound is filling the place. The preposition "through" or "across" tells you what space the sound travels through.

These three words are closely related, so it's worth separating them clearly.

Echo is specific — it means a sound bouncing back from a surface and being heard again as a copy of itself. If you shout in a canyon and hear your voice come back to you, that returned voice is an echo. Resound is broader — when a place resounds, the whole space vibrates richly with sound, not just one reflected copy.

Reverberate is the closest synonym to resound. Both mean a sound bouncing around and filling a space. The difference is subtle: reverberate is more technical and focuses on the physical bouncing of sound waves; resound is slightly more literary and also carries a figurative meaning (see below).

Plain words like "ring" or "sound" just describe a sound existing. Resound implies something more: the sound is powerful enough to fill and saturate a space. It envelops everything.

One more point: resound carries built-in intensity. A whisper doesn't resound. A soft rustle doesn't resound. The word always implies power, volume, and richness of sound.

"Resound" can also be used figuratively — not about actual sound, but about fame, impact, or significance. When something resounds in this sense, it means it is so important that it spreads far and wide, the way a powerful sound spreads through a room.

  • "His name resounded throughout history." — His fame echoed through history; he was remembered and talked about across generations.
  • "The discovery resounded across the scientific world." — The discovery was so significant that it was celebrated and discussed everywhere in science.
  • "The victory resounded across the nation." — It had such impact that the whole nation felt and talked about it.

The logic behind this is beautiful and natural: just as a great sound fills a room, a great achievement or famous name fills history or the world. The physical meaning and the figurative meaning share the same core feeling of something spreading outward and saturating everything it reaches.

This figurative use is formal and literary — you'll see it in writing, speeches, and journalism more than in everyday conversation.
What kinds of things typically resound?

Literal: Thunder, gunshots, explosions, screams, cheers, laughter, applause, bells, battle cries, music, echoes — any loud or powerful sound.

Figurative: Names, victories, discoveries, speeches, legacies, deeds — things of historical, cultural, or emotional significance.
Register — when and where you'll see this word

"Resound" is a formal, slightly literary word. It appears in novels, journalism, speeches, historical writing, and formal prose. In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "the sound echoed through," "rang out," or "filled the room." But in writing or formal contexts, resound is a precise and powerful word choice that creates a strong, vivid impression.

"Resound" means to ring out powerfully and fill a space with sound (literal), or to spread widely as something famous or impactful (figurative). The defining quality is fullness — the sound doesn't stay in one spot but saturates everything around it. The most common pattern is "a place resounded with a sound," where the place itself becomes completely filled and vibrating with that sound.
